catalog_quote: Primary stress in Omagua is penultimate, with a small number of lexical exceptions. - In morphologically simplex roots, secondary stress is assigned to alternating syllables to the left of the primary stress, as shown in Table 2. - Nouns and verbs behave the same in relation to stress. [...] An alternating pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables indicates binary feet. - Penultimate syllables are always stressed, and leftmost syllables in odd-parity words are unstressed. - We analyze this as right-aligned trochaic feet (Table 3). [...] As seen in Table 3, feet are trochaic and primary stress always falls on the head of the rightmost foot. [...] Summary of Basic Stress Derivation - Basic stress assignment in Omagua can be summarized as follows: 1. Assign right-to-left syllabic trochees to morphologically simple roots. 2. Add morphology. 3. Build a trochee at the right edge of the word. 4. Resolve stress clashes. - If possible to resolve clash by moving an old (i.e., Step 1) stress, do so. - Otherwise, delete root primary stress. - Moving or deleting penultimate stress is never possible.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (14 pp., extracted text; PDF CreationDate Sat Jan 7 2012 EST, which supports the compiler 2012 dating despite the '8 January 2011' header). p.6 §3 'Omagua Stress Assignment' bullets 1-3 read exactly: 'Primary stress in Omagua is penultimate, with a small number of lexical exceptions.' / 'In morphologically simplex roots, secondary stress is assigned to alternating syllables to the left of the primary stress, as shown in Table 2.' / 'Nouns and verbs behave the same in relation to stress.' p.7 §3.2 bullets 2-3 read exactly: 'Penultimate syllables are always stressed, and leftmost syllables in odd-parity words are unstressed.' / 'We analyze this as right-aligned trochaic feet (Table 3).…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word (nouns and verbs alike), e.g. 'kaRa 'potato', ta'paka 'piranha', tama'k1Si 'gamitana', sasa,waka'tupa 'bridge'; monosyllables are stressed. Right-aligned syllabic trochees; in odd-parity words the leftmost syllable is unfooted. Correlates: vowel length, intensity and high pitch on the primary; unstressed vowels reduce/centralize and may syncopate. When suffixes/enclitics are added, primary stress moves to the new penult while the root's secondary stresses are retained (cyclic assignment), with clash resolved by shifting a root stress one syllable left or deleting root primary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: in simplex roots on alternating syllables leftward from the penult (right-aligned trochees, e.g.,tama'k1Si, tI,puti'SiRu, sasa,waka'tupa); signalled by high pitch (lower than primary) plus some length/intensity. In morphologically complex words secondary stress reflects the root's own footing rather than a fresh alternating scan (e.g.,tamak1'Sina 'gamitanas (FS)' vs *ta,mak1'Sina), and certain six-syllable stems ending in -aRi PROG show an antepenult-penult clash (sI,nuta'ka'paRi).
new_statements.exceptions: 'a small number of lexical exceptions' (unspecified in the handout). Michael & O'Hagan 2016 p.8 add that 1PL.EXCL and 3PL free pronouns (tana, Raná/iná) carry final stress 'that is otherwise atypical within Omagua prosody', distinguishing them from the proclitics; O'Hagan 2011 p.62 notes relic final stress on a few grammatical morphemes.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (prosodic word), including suffixed/encliticized stems; data are 2-3 tokens per item elicited in a carrier frame (tsI kumIsa __ nIsupi 'I say __ to you') from one elderly speaker of San Joaquín de Omaguas, Loreto, Peru; fn.6 notes phrase-initial first-syllable lengthening. The 2016 monograph separately notes that 'long' vowels are doubled monomoraic vowels because the penultimate pattern targets the second vowel (kuu vs ku'una).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Peruvian Omagua as spoken by the last elderly speakers of San Joaquín de Omaguas (Loreto, Peru), i.e. omag1248 proper (the 'modern Omagua' of the Berkeley Omagua Documentation Project). The other opened phonology, Souza dos Santos 2015 (UFAM MA thesis), describes the Brazilian Omágua/Kambeba variety of Tururukari-Uka (Manacapuru, Amazonas), a resurgent/heritage variety, and reports stress as unpredictable between penult and final syllable — the two descriptions differ; Glottolog treats Kambeba under the same code omag1248 (ISO omg), so no separate glottocode is given here. Note also that Glottolog dates the IJAL sketch 2019, but Crossref and the authors' CVs give 2020, 86(1):95-131.

sources.quote: p. 8: "In the 1pl and 3pl, free pronouns and proclitics are distinguished via stress placement, where the former receive a final stress that is otherwise atypical within Omagua prosody. [...] In the 1incl, neither length, stress or form distinguish the free pronoun from proclitic; such distinctions may only be made based on whether yini(=) forms a prosodic word with its host, that is, whether it is assigned its own stress or falls within the domain of stress assignment of the verbal stem." p. 8: "Old Omagua does not appear to distinguish via stress placement the pronominal and proclitic forms of the 1pl.excl and 3pl as the modern language does; only penultimate stress is attested on these forms." pp. 17-18: "It is part of a small class of monosyllabic grammatical morphemes in the language that attract their own stress, yielding final stress, a pattern that is otherwise atypical within Kokama-Kokamilla and Omagua prosody (Vallejos Yopán (2010a:119-124), Sandy and O'Hagan (2012b)). All other members of this class of morphemes historically exhibited an additional syllable that explains their synchronically aberrant stress pattern (O'Hagan and Wauters 2012), i.e., with an additional fi
sources.locator: printed p. 8, Section 2.2.1.1 with fn. 20; printed pp. 17-18, Section 2.2.2 discussion of =aRi, fn. 42; printed p. 40, fn. 85
sources.note: No dedicated stress section; Section 2.1 (Phonological Inventory, pp. 6-7) covers segments only. The stress system is stated in passing: the expected pattern is right-aligned trochaic yielding penultimate stress, and final stress is 'atypical within Omagua prosody'; the modern stress analysis is credited to the authors' own handout Sandy and O'Hagan (2012b), which is the catalog's primary cite. Secondary stress: not stated. Weight: p. 8 and fn. 20 report a bimoraic minimum word requirement on nouns (kuu [ku:] 'swidden' vs kuuna [ku"una]); no weight-sensitivity of stress stated. Domain: the pro
